objectives: Conclude an Article XXVIII package with the UK in time for the June Council sequence, while preserving the core of the notified modification: a real bound rate, a controllable TRQ, and a permanent legal footing against non-market-economy overcapacity.

Buy UK acceptance primarily through steel-access calibration rather than broad tariff concessions elsewhere: volume, allocation, administration, product carve-outs, duration/review, circumvention language and FTA/TCA treatment are preferred currencies.
Prevent the UK from joining or fronting a Japan/Korea-led FTA dispute or retaliation track; keep Turkey, Korea, India and Japan in separate lanes and avoid multilateralising the steel file.

Use linkage to the UK's own steel measure and Article XXVIII process, where EU exporters hold country-specific quotas and supply 3.6 million tonnes to the UK, to make reciprocity explicit without turning the negotiation into a wider trade war.

Protect the EU's long-term Geneva position: demonstrate Article XXVIII discipline, keep compensation defensible, avoid precedent that FTA tariff reductions can be casually disapplied, and leave working relations intact for other goods files.
declaration.success_and_failure: Success is a same-terms settlement accepted by Brussels and London by round four, or at minimum a controlled non-settlement in which the modification proceeds on schedule, the UK does not join an FTA retaliation/disapplication coalition, and any UK rebalancing is narrow, delayed and manageable. Failure is a June timeline slip, UK withdrawal of substantially equivalent concessions against EU exports, a coordinated UK-Japan-Korea FTA dispute, erosion of the measure through an oversized or poorly administered TRQ, or a Geneva precedent that damages the EU's credibility on schedules and FTAs.
declaration.approach: Open by affirming the UK's principal supplying interest and the EU's intention to negotiate seriously, while being clear the modification itself is not in doubt. Move the UK quickly from abstract injury to concrete parameters: quota size, allocation method, administration, out-of-quota rate, review, carve-outs, enforcement and TCA/FTA interface. Signal early that a global first-come-first-served 400,000 tonne TRQ is especially bad for concentrated UK suppliers and that the EU can explore more predictable access if the UK accepts the legal architecture and restrained rebalancing. Privately frame FTA disapplication as a negotiable design feature rather than an ideological line, provided any FTA-compatible fix is narrow, origin-secure and not extended into a general precedent. Keep compensation off non-steel lines unless needed to close, and use the UK's exposure on EU steel imports and its own safeguard process to argue for symmetry and calm. Throughout, report tightly to Brussels, keep other claimants separate, and make every offer conditional on no UK participation in FTA retaliation or joint dispute action.

parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: Maximum tariff-free access for 2.4 million tonnes of UK steel exports, country-specific or otherwise predictable quota shares, no disapplication of EU-UK TCA preferences, product carve-outs for concentrated UK lines, and linkage to EU treatment under the UK's own steel measure.

parties.who: UK capital: Department for Business and Trade and ministers
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: A politically saleable outcome for a small number of high-employment steel sites, avoidance of sudden first-come-first-served disruption, and enough leverage preserved to show the EU did not simply impose the measure.
A legally clean Article XXVIII process concluded on mandate, no uncontrolled compensation bill, no FTA precedent that invites disputes, and a reportable path to Council approval by June.

parties.who: Council and Trade Policy Committee member states
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: Steel-producing member states will want a tight quota, high out-of-quota protection and strong anti-circumvention; steel-consuming member states will want adequate import supply and no escalation with the UK that hits manufacturing inputs.

parties.who: EU steel industry and downstream users
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: Producers want durable protection from overcapacity and minimal UK leakage through preferences; downstream users want stable access to imported semi-finished and specialty grades and no retaliatory spiral.
A country-specific allocation close to historic EU-bound volumes, licensing rather than first-come-first-served, exemptions for niche products, and preservation of TCA benefits.
Separate compensation and access improvements; Korea and Japan may also test whether FTA disapplication creates a coalition opportunity, so they will watch whether the UK is bought off or isolated.

Procedural compliance, transparency, and avoidance of a visible rupture between schedules, safeguards and FTA obligations; the EU must look like it is using Article XXVIII properly rather than improvising protectionism.

objectives: Secure UK acceptance of the Article XXVIII modification within four rounds so the Council can vote in June and the regime enters into force on schedule.

Preserve the core protective effect of the regime: a binding out-of-quota rate at or near 50% and a total zero-duty volume low enough to deliver a significant, visible reduction in steel imports. Volume is my most guarded variable.

Avoid any structure that sets an unmanageable precedent for the parallel Turkey, Korea, India and Japan claims — anything conceded to the UK must be defensible as case-specific compensation, not a template.

Protect EU exporters' position under the UK's own steel measure and Article XXVIII process — ideally by trading improved UK access for UK restraint on the country-specific quotas EU mills currently rely on (3.6Mt of EU exports are at stake).

Keep the deal politically sellable to the TPC: steel-producing member states must see real import restraint; consuming member states and the UK Mission must see a stable, administered quota rather than chaotic first-come-first-served allocation.
Avoid adding to the EU's short-term economic exposure given the US retaliation threats — a clean, quick EU-UK settlement removes one front.
declaration.success_and_failure: Success: a signed Article XXVIII agreement within the four rounds that the Council can endorse in June, with an out-of-quota bound rate no lower than ~40-50%, total zero-duty access (global plus any UK share) not far above the notified 400kt, country-specific UK allocation framed as compensation rather than preference, and at least an informal UK understanding on EU treatment under its own measure. Partial success: agreement reached but with a UK quota large enough to erode the import-reduction objective — sellable, but I will be answerable for regime performance. Failure: no agreement. The UK walks, the June Council slot is lost, the measure slips months, and the US threat compounds; even though no-deal hurts UK steel more, I will have failed my instruction to secure agreement on schedule and the regime's launch will look chaotic. Worst case: a late, panicked concession of a large UK carve-out plus FTA pool access that collapses the protective effect and triggers copycat demands from Ankara, Seoul, Delhi and Tokyo.
declaration.approach: Open firm: defend the 400kt global first-come-first-served design and the 50% rate as necessary against non-market overcapacity, and probe what the UK actually needs — my working assumption is certainty of access, not unlimited volume. Concede early on the cheap items that cost the regime little: move from first-come-first-served to licensing/administered allocation (good for predictability, no volume cost), offer a review clause and duration language, and signal flexibility on product-line carve-outs for UK-specialist grades where the UK is the dominant supplier and volumes are small. Hold volume tight: any UK country-specific quota should be modest (a few hundred thousand tonnes, phased, with carry-over and circumvention safeguards) and presented as the compensation package itself, explicitly without prejudice to other Article XXVIII claims. Use the linkage deliberately: improved UK terms are conditioned on constructive treatment of EU exporters in the UK's own process — this is my strongest leverage and the one thing that justifies generosity to the Council. Slow-walk the FTA disapplication text rather than trading it cheaply; dropping or softening it is a late-round concession to close the deal. Manage the clock openly: remind the UK privately through my Geneva seat that no-deal devastates UK steel (75% of exports, concentrated sites) while the EU merely loses a Council slot — their time pressure is worse than mine, but I must not overplay this because I genuinely need the June vote. Reserve any meaningful volume increase for the final round and tie it to UK restraint on its own measure.

parties.who: UK Geneva seat (UK Mission to WTO)
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: Maximum guaranteed zero-duty access for UK mills — a large country-specific quota or full carve-out — plus deletion of the FTA-disapplication text. They will stress principal-supplying-interest status, the existential risk to UK steel sites, and their six-month right to withdraw equivalent concessions. Expect them to hint at linkage to the TCA and to their own measure's treatment of EU steel.

parties.who: UK capital (Department for Business and Trade / ministers)
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: A politically defensible deal protecting concentrated steel employment before any deadline, but with real red lines on volume; ministers need to show they did not fold. They know no-deal is catastrophic for them, so they are ultimately likely to settle if given a face-saving country-specific quota and some review/carve-out language.

parties.who: European Commission / Commissioner and my DG TRADE hierarchy
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: Delivery of the mandate on time with the regime's protective effect intact; no precedent that complicates the other four claims; no new exposure while the US threat is live.

Steel-producing states: deep import cuts, scepticism of any UK carve-out, insistence on circumvention enforcement. Consuming/manufacturing states: predictable supply, licensing administration, lower rates. Both: no slippage past June.

parties.who: EU steel industry and downstream users
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: Industry: minimal TRQ volume, high out-of-quota rate, tight anti-circumvention. Users: stability, licensing, product carve-outs for grades not made in the EU. They will lobby capitals against any generosity to the UK.

Watching every concession for precedent value; Turkey and Korea will demand at least UK-equivalent treatment by volume. Any UK-specific share must be justifiable on principal-supplying-interest and product-concentration grounds they cannot replicate.
Not a party, but their retaliation threat raises the cost of a prolonged, messy process and strengthens the case for a fast, quiet EU-UK settlement.

Room to manoeuvre and credible fallback language; will want clear instructions on what can be floated versus what is capital-only, and may be more inclined than me to buy a deal with volume — I must keep the leash on the total zero-duty tonnage.

objectives: Secure the largest possible duty-free quota volume for UK steel into the EU, ideally well above the 400,000 tonne opening, and as close as possible to covering the UK's 2.4 million tonnes of annual exports
Obtain a UK-specific country allocation or other guaranteed access mechanism rather than a global first-come first-served quota that Turkish and Korean volumes would exhaust early in the year
Remove or substantially soften the disapplication of FTA tariff reductions for UK-origin steel, preserving TCA preferential treatment
Lower the out-of-quota bound rate below 50% and secure a review clause and defined duration so the measure is not a permanent ceiling on UK access
Conclude a settlement by June that London can defend politically, avoiding the no-deal outcome which leaves UK steel with near-total loss of tariff-free EU access
Protect the working relationship with my EU counterpart across the wider goods file, and avoid being dragged by Japan and Korea into an FTA dispute strategy that would poison the negotiation
declaration.success_and_failure: Success is a settled package by Round 4 that gives the UK a guaranteed duty-free volume covering a substantial share of current exports (through a country-specific allocation, licensing, or enlarged global quota), an out-of-quota rate meaningfully below 50%, FTA disapplication removed or narrowed, and a review clause — such that London accepts and the industry survives. Failure is no settlement, or a settlement so thin that London rejects it, leaving the 400,000 tonne global FCFS quota at 50% to take effect and the UK steel industry facing structural collapse; a secondary failure is wrecking my broader Geneva working relationships or letting Japan and Korea's dispute agenda derail the bilateral track for no UK gain.
declaration.approach: Open firm and specific, as instructed and as I believe: reject the opening offer as unacceptable, anchor high with a concrete UK ask (UK-specific allocation sized near current trade volumes, TCA treatment preserved, lower out-of-quota rate), and make the EU justify every element of its proposal. Use the EU's June Council deadline as leverage — they need this concluded on schedule, I can afford patience within the four rounds. Hold back flexibility until the EU shows real movement, and trade concessions deliberately: UK movement on its own steel measure treatment of EU exporters and on administration method in exchange for volume, allocation, and FTA-treatment gains. Probe what the EU can actually offer on compensation elsewhere in the schedule as a secondary channel. Keep Japan and Korea at arm's length — listen, do not commit, and do not let their dispute strategy become my negotiating position. Report honestly to London each round so capital can calibrate, given I have no settlement figure and must construct the landing zone through the negotiation itself.

parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: Conclude by June with a defensible compensation package; preserve as much of the 50%/400,000t structure as possible; balance steel-producing member states against steel-consuming ones; keep the TRQ design flexible enough to survive the Council vote; manage parallel claims from Turkey, Korea, India and Japan without the UK deal setting an expensive precedent.

A settlement that prevents destruction of the UK steel industry, defensible to ministers and to steel-producing constituencies; will push hard on volume and allocation; may be tempted by retaliation threats but ultimately needs a deal because no-deal is catastrophic.

A package within the negotiating mandate, legally durable, acceptable to both steel-producing and steel-consuming member states, concluded on the June timeline; reluctant to carve out FTA partners or grant large country-specific quotas that inflate Turkey and Korea's parallel claims.

To recruit the UK into a joint FTA dispute and retaliation strategy against the EU, using UK dissatisfaction to add pressure in their own separate Article XXVIII claims; indifferent to UK steel's specific exposure.

Maximum duty-free access for their own larger volumes; Turkey especially benefits from a global FCFS quota and will resist UK-specific allocations that shrink the residual pool; pursuing their claims separately.

parties.who: UK steel industry and producing-site constituencies
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: Guaranteed, predictable duty-free access to the EU covering the bulk of the 2.4 million tonnes; political pressure on London not to settle for crumbs.

objectives: Secure a UK country-specific TRQ allocation sized as close as possible to historical trade (target 1.5–2.0 million tonnes; minimum acceptable floor around 1.2 million tonnes) rather than a global first-come-first-served quota in which UK volumes would be crowded out by Turkey, Korea and others

Delete or substantially narrow the proposed legal text disapplying FTA/TCA tariff preferences for UK-origin steel — this is the single most damaging element of the EU proposal and is arguably inconsistent with the TCA
Reduce the out-of-quota bound rate well below 50% (target 20–25%), and/or secure carve-outs for product lines where the UK is the dominant supplier and EU import dependence is high
Secure a review clause and defined duration so the regime is not locked in permanently at punitive levels

Preserve the ability to deploy the Minister's subsidisation package and the UK's own safeguard quotas as leverage, while keeping any UK concessions on EU safeguard allocations strictly conditional and reciprocal
Avoid a no-deal outcome in which the UK must retaliate six months later — retaliation damages EU exporters but does not save the two at-risk UK plants
declaration.success_and_failure: Success: a settlement giving the UK a guaranteed country-specific allocation covering a substantial majority of our 2.4Mt historical trade, removal or dilution of the FTA-disapplication clause, an out-of-quota rate materially below 50%, and a review clause — enough that Ministers can present the deal as securing the industry's core EU market and the plant owners have reason to invest. Partial success: a good quota volume but surviving FTA-disapplication text, compensated by concessions elsewhere in the EU schedule plus our subsidy package. Failure: a global first-come-first-served quota, FTA preferences disapplied, 50% out-of-quota rate, and no review — in which case the two plants likely close, Ministers are politically exposed, and I am accountable for a negotiation that achieved nothing beyond what no-deal would have delivered anyway. I will also judge the deal on whether I kept the EU's parallel claims from Turkey and Korea from eroding our share, and whether any UK safeguard concessions given up were matched pound-for-pound by EU movement.
declaration.approach: Negotiate from leverage, not grievance. My strongest card is that the EU exports 3.6Mt of steel to the UK — more than we export to them — and EU exporters currently hold country-specific quotas in our own safeguard regime. I will make clear early that improved EU allocations under the UK measure are available only in exchange for a UK country-specific allocation and removal of the FTA-disapplication text, and that if the EU proceeds on its notified terms, the UK will withdraw substantially equivalent concessions calibrated to hit EU steel and politically sensitive member-state exports. I will also exploit the EU's internal tension: steel-consuming member states and manufacturers have an interest in continued UK supply, and the Commission needs this concluded by June to hold its Council timetable — time pressure is on their side, not ours. Tactically, I will open ambitiously (full carve-out of UK volumes via a bilateral understanding anchored in the TCA), concede slowly, package rather than trade item-by-item, and reserve the subsidy announcement as a domestic cushion that lets me walk away from a genuinely bad deal rather than sign it. Throughout, I will keep the FTA-disapplication clause framed as a legal and trust problem under the TCA, not merely a commercial one, because that gives the Commission a face-saving reason to drop it.

parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: To execute my instructions faithfully at the table, read the Commission's room for movement accurately, and report back candidly. They may be more conciliatory than I am, valuing the Geneva relationship; I need them to hold the line on country-specific allocation and the FTA clause without freelancing.

A quick, clean conclusion by June that keeps the 50% bound rate and a modest TRQ, minimal bespoke treatment for the UK that would complicate their parallel Article XXVIII negotiations with Turkey, Korea, India and Japan, and no precedent that FTA partners get preferential treatment. They will resist a country-specific UK share precisely because Turkey and Korea would then demand the same.

Divided. Steel-producing states want maximum protection; steel-consuming states and those exporting steel to the UK want stability and fear UK retaliation against their exports. I want to amplify that division.

parties.who: UK steel industry and plant owners
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: A guaranteed, sizeable EU quota with a low out-of-quota rate — certainty over volume matters more to them than headline tariff numbers. The owners of the two at-risk plants are making an investment decision on the back of this outcome.
Cheap EU steel imports into the UK; they will resist me hardening the UK safeguard as leverage. I must manage them domestically so their lobbying does not undercut my negotiating position.

A politically presentable deal that keeps plants open and lets them claim they saved the industry; they will accept concessions elsewhere in the schedule if the headline on steel is defensible, but will not forgive a capitulation.
Their own maximal quotas; a UK country-specific carve-out shrinks the global pool available to them, so anything I win bilaterally may be contested indirectly through pressure on the Commission.

public_message:
Thank you, and thank you to the UK delegation. The European Union opens this negotiation under Article XXVIII on the basis of our notified intention to modify bound rates on these 41 steel tariff lines. Let me set out our position and how we hope to proceed.

First, context. This measure responds to structural global overcapacity driven by non-market economy production — a pressure the UK steel industry knows as well as ours, and one your own safeguard process also addresses. It is not aimed at the United Kingdom, a market-economy partner and our closest steel relationship.

Our notified position is a bound out-of-quota rate of 50 per cent, with a tariff rate quota of 400,000 tonnes per year, allocated globally on a first-come, first-served basis. We table that as the starting point, as the Article XXVIII process requires. But we recognize the United Kingdom holds a principal supplying interest in these lines, and we come to negotiate, not simply to notify. The volume of the quota, the method and administration of allocation, duration and review, product coverage, and compensation elsewhere in our schedule are all open for discussion. We are prepared to examine arrangements that reflect the UK's specific trade position as part of an overall balance.

Two further points. First, the matters on the table include the treatment of EU exporters under the UK's own steel measure, where EU suppliers currently hold country-specific allocations. We see value in addressing the two processes in parallel, with reciprocal predictability for exporters on both sides of the Channel. Second, on the interaction with the EU-UK TCA: we would strongly prefer to resolve that interaction within this negotiation, in a manner that preserves the integrity of our agreement, rather than see it litigated. A cooperative outcome here serves both sides; an escalatory one would not.

We would now welcome the United Kingdom's position: the volume and allocation you seek, your views on administration, duration and review, and any compensation interests you wish to register.

other_terms: Notified FTA preference disapplication remains part of the package, but its application to UK-origin steel is explicitly open to negotiation within this process
All design parameters (volume, allocation, administration, duration, review, product coverage) stated as open for discussion
Compensation on other lines in the EU schedule available for discussion
Proposal to address the EU and UK steel measures in parallel, with reciprocal treatment of exporters as an organising principle

expectations.what_you_expect_next: A maximalist opening: TRQ volume at or near current UK export levels (2.4Mt), a country-specific UK allocation, an out-of-quota rate well below 50%, a review clause, and registered compensation demands. Likely invocation of the TCA and a hint at dispute options to build leverage.
expectations.why: Standard opening posture given severe domestic exposure (75% of UK steel exports) and the need to show UK industry a hard line; they will also test whether the FTA disapplication text is a red line.

expectations.what_you_expect_next: An attempt to link their asks to the treatment of EU exporters under the UK's own safeguard measure, holding EU country-specific allocations there as counter-leverage.
expectations.why: It is their strongest card — 3.6Mt of EU exports into the UK market — and they will want reciprocity framed explicitly.

expectations.who: Third parties (Japan, Korea) via UK delegation
expectations.what_you_expect_next: The UK may float the prospect of coordinated action on the FTA disapplication to pressure us into carving FTA partners out.
expectations.why: We have indications Japan and Korea are recruiting the UK into a joint dispute; the UK may use that threat implicitly even if it does not intend to join.

private_rationale: I have no settlement figure from Brussels, so Round 1 must anchor on the notified measure (50% / 400,000t / global FCFS) while signalling flexibility on every design parameter. This achieves three things. First, it elicits the UK's full position — volume, allocation, rate, compensation — which I am instructed to report back. Second, by publicly stating that FTA treatment of UK-origin steel is negotiable and that we prefer to resolve the TCA interaction inside this process rather than through litigation, I undercut the Japan/Korea recruitment effort: the UK needs to see a cooperative path that preserves its TCA access, which is worth far more to it than a joint dispute. Third, I plant the parallelism frame — a UK tranche in our measure traded against security for EU country-specific allocations in theirs — which is the natural shape of the eventual deal and the EU's best leverage. I deliberately avoid numbers beyond the notification (no tranche figure, no revised volume) so I concede nothing before Brussels gives me room; equally I avoid making the FTA disapplication a public red line, since that is precisely the coalition trigger. Restating global allocation now preserves the country-specific concession as a tradeable for later rounds, at most signalling it verbally as examinable. Review clause and duration are held in reserve as cheap concessions.

public_message:
Thank you, and thank you to the EU delegation. The United Kingdom welcomes the constructive framing, and we agree on one thing at the outset: this measure responds to non-market economy overcapacity, and it would be perverse if its principal casualty were a market-economy partner facing the identical pressure. Yet on the notified terms, that is precisely the outcome. The UK shipped an average of 2.4 million tonnes a year into this market over the representative period — 75 per cent of our steel exports by value, concentrated in a narrow product range where we are, on many of these lines, the EU's principal or only significant external supplier. A 400,000-tonne global first-come, first-served pool does not compensate for the withdrawal of zero-bound access on that trade; it eliminates it. Global FCFS allocation would see the quota exhausted within weeks by the very non-market volumes this measure purports to target, leaving established UK producers with a 50 per cent out-of-quota wall. I want to be plain: that outcome is not a negotiating position we can work within. It is the destruction of the UK steel industry, and London regards it as such.

The United Kingdom therefore opens as follows. First, volume: the total pool must be sized against actual trade, not against an administrative number. We propose a total quota of 3 million tonnes. Second, allocation: country-specific, with a UK tranche of 2.4 million tonnes reflecting the representative period, administered by licensing with quarterly release and carryover of unused tonnage — first-come, first-served on a global basis is not administrable and rewards speed of shipment over established trade. Third, the out-of-quota rate: 50 per cent is prohibitive, not protective. We propose 15 per cent. Fourth, duration and review: three years, with a mandatory review clause. Fifth, product coverage: we will table a list of lines where UK supply is dominant and EU domestic production is minimal, which should be carved out entirely. Sixth, and I must be direct on this: the proposed disapplication of FTA tariff reductions for UK-originating steel is not a matter for negotiation within Article XXVIII. It is a breach of the EU-UK Trade and Cooperation Agreement, and the UK reserves all its rights under that agreement, including the dispute settlement provisions. We note we are not the only FTA partner taking that view. We would strongly counsel the EU to withdraw that element rather than have it become the defining feature of this process. Finally, on your point about parallel treatment: we are open to discussing reciprocal predictability for EU exporters under the UK's own measure — but on the basis of balance, and only once the shape of the EU's offer is one we can describe to London as serious.

We look forward to the EU's response on each of these elements.

other_terms: Withdrawal of the proposed disapplication of FTA/TCA tariff reductions for UK-originating steel
Licensed administration with quarterly release and carryover of unused tranche tonnage
Carve-out of tariff lines where UK is the dominant supplier and EU domestic production is minimal, list to be tabled
Compensation on other lines in the EU schedule to be registered, pending the EU's response on volume and allocation
Reciprocal predictability for EU exporters under the UK steel measure to be addressed in parallel, contingent on overall balance

expectations.what_you_expect_next: A counter that moves on total volume (perhaps to 800,000–1.2 million tonnes) but resists country-specific allocation, citing Turkey and Korea's larger volumes and MFN optics, and defends the FTA disapplication as within the EU's rights under Article XXVIII.
expectations.why: The EU must balance five claimants and its own member states split between steel producers and steel consumers; it will concede volume before conceding allocation method, because a UK-specific tranche invites identical demands from Ankara and Seoul.

expectations.what_you_expect_next: Confirmation that the opening anchors are approved and guidance on which elements are genuinely tradeable — I expect licensing administration and duration to be more flexible than tranche size and the TCA point.
expectations.why: London has no settlement figure yet and instructed firmness; they will want to see the EU's first move before authorizing any concession.

expectations.what_you_expect_next: Renewed pressure on capital colleagues to join a joint FTA dispute, especially once my public reservation of TCA rights signals the UK is keeping that route open.
expectations.why: My statement that 'we are not the only FTA partner taking that view' gives them a hook without committing the UK to coordination.

private_rationale: I opened at the top of a credible envelope: full restoration of UK trade volumes as a country-specific tranche, a pool sized to real trade, and a 15 per cent out-of-quota rate, while staking the TCA disapplication as a legal red line rather than a negotiating chip. This anchors the bargaining range around UK trade reality (2.4 Mt) rather than the EU's administrative fiction (0.4 Mt), and my remit guidance — firmness pays, early flexibility invites demands — argues against conceding anything in Round 1. I deliberately did not table compensation asks on other lines yet: registering them now would signal I expect to lose on the core steel terms. I flagged the TCA dispute route and the existence of other aggrieved FTA partners to raise the cost of the EU's disapplication provision without committing to the Japan/Korea joint action — that remains leverage in reserve, and deploying it now would harden the Commission and alarm steel-consuming member states whose support I need in Council. The linkage to EU exporters under the UK measure I acknowledged but explicitly gated behind a serious EU offer, since that is my strongest card and must not be traded early. The June Council deadline cuts both ways: the EU needs conclusion, but I must not appear to need it, so I framed no-deal as unacceptable for the EU's own market stability rather than as a UK vulnerability.

report: Round 1 opened with both sides tabling maximalist positions. I set out the notified terms (50% bound rate, 400,000t global FCFS quota) as the starting point, flagged that volume, allocation, administration, duration, review, carve-outs and compensation are all open, and signalled EU interest in parallel treatment of the two steel processes and in resolving the TCA interaction within this negotiation rather than through litigation. The UK responded with a very high opening demand: a total pool of 3 million tonnes; a country-specific UK tranche of 2.4 million tonnes (their full representative-period trade); licensing with quarterly release and carryover; an out-of-quota rate of 15%; three-year duration with mandatory review; and carve-outs on lines where UK supply is dominant. On allocation they were categorical: global FCFS is unacceptable to them, on the grounds that non-market volumes would exhaust the pool within weeks — this is their strongest and most credible point, and aligns with the measure's stated rationale. They also stated firmly that the proposed disapplication of FTA tariff reductions for UK steel is, in their view, a breach of the TCA, reserved all rights including dispute settlement, noted pointedly that they are not the only FTA partner taking that view, and counselled us to withdraw that element. They held out reciprocal predictability for EU exporters under their own measure, but only once our offer is 'serious'. No convergence yet, but both sides engaged on all elements and the UK did not walk away from the table.

recommendation.reasoning: Neither opening is a landing zone. The UK's ask (3Mt pool, 2.4Mt UK tranche, 15% OQR) would hollow out the measure and is not saleable to steel-producing member states; our notified position is, as the UK says, not compensatory for their trade and they are a principal supplying interest we must accommodate meaningfully. The credible zone of agreement, in my judgement, is: country-specific allocation (we should concede this early — it serves our own anti-circumvention logic and is the UK's existential ask), a total pool well above 400,000t but well below 3Mt (I suggest we explore 1.0–1.5Mt), a UK tranche reflecting a substantial share of their representative trade but not 100% (0.8–1.1Mt), an OQR between 20–35%, duration of 4–6 years with a review clause (low cost to us, high value to them). I recommend continuing on roughly the indicative terms above as an exploratory envelope, while making clear to London that the 2.4Mt/15% combination is unreachable. Carve-outs and compensation on other lines can be used to close the gap at the end. Separately, the FTA-disapplication clause is generating serious escalation risk: the UK explicitly hinted at coordination with other FTA partners, consistent with the whisperings about Japan and Korea. I strongly recommend we seek authority to signal flexibility on that clause — or to trade its withdrawal as a major concession — rather than let it trigger a joint TCA/FTA dispute that would dwarf the value of the steel measure.

requests.what_you_are_asking_for: A settlement envelope from the Council: floor and ceiling on total quota volume (proposed 1.0–1.5Mt), UK tranche (0.8–1.1Mt), OQR (20–35%), and duration (4–6 years with review), so I can move off the notified position without tabling numbers I cannot defend.
requests.why: I currently have no settlement figure. The UK will not engage seriously until we table a move, and I cannot calibrate the first concession without knowing Brussels' red lines and member-state tolerances.

instruction: Good read of the room. You are authorised to move off the notified position in Round 2, in a sequenced way. First, concede country-specific allocation early and present it as our own logic: the measure targets non-market economy overcapacity, and a global FCFS pool would be exhausted by precisely those volumes — allocation by country serves the measure's stated purpose and our anti-circumvention interest. This is the UK's existential ask and costs us less than volume does. Second, table an exploratory envelope, not a final offer: total pool in the region of 1.0–1.3 million tonnes; UK tranche in the region of 800,000–1,000,000 tonnes administered by licensing with quarterly release (carryover we can discuss, capped); out-of-quota rate of 25–35% — do not go below 25% without further authority; duration five years with a review clause at mid-term. Make unmistakably clear that 2.4Mt/15% is unreachable and would not survive the Council. Third, on the FTA-disapplication clause: you are authorised to signal flexibility — indicate we are prepared to revisit the clause as part of an overall settlement, but do not offer outright withdrawal yet; hold it as a trade against UK movement on volume/OQR or on their safeguard measure. If pressed, you may indicate that limiting its scope (e.g., preserving TCA preferences within the UK tranche) is conceivable. Do not concede it for nothing: it is our largest single bargaining chip and the UK has told us so. Fourth, on linkage: engage on parallel treatment of the UK safeguard measure informally. State that the EU would expect, as part of a balanced outcome, preservation of EU country-specific allocations under the UK measure at current volumes and no shift to global FCFS on their side. Do not formalise the linkage in text yet; keep it as mutual predictability. Fifth, probe their carve-out list — ask them to table it — but make no commitments; carve-outs are endgame material, as are compensation lines, which I am having identified now. Do not table any compensation lines in Round 2. Your posture: constructive, moving, but firm that both sides must travel; remind them privately that no-deal means 400,000t global FCFS and a 50% wall, which their industry feels far more than ours, and that a June conclusion is in both sides' interest.

authority.notes: These are ceilings/floors for Round 2 tabling, not settlement authority. Total pool: do not exceed 1.3Mt; UK tranche: do not exceed 1.0Mt; OQR: do not go below 25%. Licensing administration with quarterly release is acceptable; carryover of unused tonnage may be conceded capped (e.g., one quarter). Review clause at mid-term (year 3 of 5) is acceptable. FTA-disapplication clause: authorised to signal flexibility and discuss scope limitation, not authorised to withdraw outright without further clearance. Carve-outs and compensation lines: probing only, no commitments. Linkage to UK safeguard measure: informal discussion authorised, seeking preservation of EU country-specific allocations at current volumes; no formal text linkage without clearance.

report: Round 1 was an exchange of opening positions, as expected. The EU tabled its notified position (50% bound rate, 400,000t global FCFS quota) explicitly as a starting point and signalled flexibility on all core elements: volume, allocation method and administration, duration and review, product coverage, and compensation elsewhere in the schedule. They framed the measure as targeting non-market overcapacity, not the UK, and said they are prepared to examine arrangements reflecting the UK's specific trade position. Two notable linkages from their side: (1) they explicitly connected this negotiation to the treatment of EU exporters under our own steel measure, seeking reciprocal predictability — i.e., they want a two-sided deal, which gives us leverage; and (2) they expressed a strong preference to resolve the TCA interaction within this negotiation rather than see it litigated — a tell that the FTA disapplication element is legally uncomfortable for them and potentially tradable or withdrawable. I opened hard as instructed: 3Mt total pool, country-specific allocation with a 2.4Mt UK tranche based on the representative period, licensing administration with quarterly release and carryover, 15% out-of-quota rate, three years with mandatory review, carve-outs on lines where UK supply is dominant and EU production minimal. I put down a firm marker that FTA disapplication is a breach of the TCA, that we reserve all rights including dispute settlement, and that we are not the only FTA partner taking that view — without committing to the joint action Japan and Korea are pressing for. I signalled conditional openness on reciprocal treatment for EU exporters under our measure, but only against a serious EU offer. No numbers were exchanged by the EU beyond their notified position; no terms are yet on the table that could be accepted or rejected.

recommendation.reasoning: There is nothing to accept yet — the EU has tabled only its notified position and asked for ours. Accepting is not available; walking away after one round would forfeit the two clearest pressure points we identified (their desire to avoid TCA litigation and their interest in protecting EU exporters' access under our own measure) and would leave us facing the notified terms, which London has assessed as fatal to the industry. The EU's language ('prepared to examine arrangements that reflect the UK's specific trade position') suggests country-specific allocation is within their contemplation. We should hold our opening position in Round 2 and press them to put actual numbers on volume and allocation before we move anything. Their June Council deadline is our friend: each round that passes without progress raises their cost of no-deal, while our worst case is already the notified terms, so time pressure is asymmetric in our favour so long as London can tolerate the no-deal risk.

You read the table correctly: the EU's two linkages (reciprocal treatment under our own measure; avoiding TCA litigation) are our leverage, and their June deadline works for us. Round 2 guidance: HOLD the full opening position without conceding any element. Press them to table concrete numbers on total volume and allocation method before we move on anything — make clear that 'prepared to examine arrangements' is not a position and that London cannot engage seriously until the EU puts figures on the table. On the TCA: maintain the firm marker that disapplication is a breach and must be withdrawn; you may note, without overcommitting, that a cooperative resolution here makes that element unnecessary. Licensing administration with quarterly release and carryover is preferred but is ultimately tradable if the tranche is country-specific and near representative volumes. The political reality: two plants are on the brink, and a deal below roughly 1.8Mt country-specific will be very hard to sell as saving them — though the subsidy programme gives us a fallback that lets us sign a thinner tariff deal if compensation elsewhere is large enough. I am not telling Geneva that yet; they negotiate better believing volume is existential. The EU's June deadline and their visible anxiety on the TCA point argue for patience — our worst case is the notified terms, which we already face, while their worst case is a collapsed schedule, TCA litigation from multiple FTA partners, and retaliation from their largest steel export market. Holding firm in Round 2 is low-risk. The linkage to our own safeguard is genuinely valuable to them (3.6Mt of EU exports to us) and I have authority to spend it, but it must be spent last and against their biggest concessions — a UK tranche near 2.4Mt and disapplication withdrawn. reasoning: There are no agreed terms to accept: the EU notified 400,000 tonnes global FCFS at 50%, while the UK opened at a 3 million tonne pool, 2.4 million tonne UK tranche and 15% out-of-quota rate. Neither position is a viable landing zone. A negotiated outcome remains preferable because lapse would prevent the Council voting in June, even though the UK would bear heavier immediate damage. Brussels has authorised a Round 2 move: concede country-specific allocation early, explore a total pool up to 1.3 million tonnes, a UK tranche up to 1.0 million tonnes, licensing with quarterly release, an out-of-quota rate no lower than 25%, five-year duration and a mid-term review, while holding back FTA-disapplication withdrawal, carve-outs and compensation lines for later leverage.

No acceptable negotiated package is currently on the table. The EU has only restated its notified starting position of 400,000 tonnes allocated globally on a first-come, first-served basis with a 50% out-of-quota rate, which would be severely damaging to UK steel exports and is unacceptable. The EU has signalled flexibility on volume, allocation, administration, review and compensation, and its interest in reciprocal treatment under the UK measure and avoiding TCA litigation gives the UK leverage. We should therefore continue, hold the opening position, and require the EU to table concrete numbers before making any movement.

public_message:
Thank you. The EU has listened carefully, and we come back with a substantive move — not a restatement. Let me take the elements in turn.

First, allocation. You argued that a global first-come, first-served pool would be exhausted within weeks by precisely the non-market volumes this measure targets. You are right, and frankly that argument is our argument. A measure aimed at non-market overcapacity that administers its quota in a way that privileges speed of shipment over established market-economy trade would be self-defeating. The EU is therefore prepared to move from global allocation to country-specific allocation, administered by import licensing with quarterly release. We take your point on carryover and are prepared to discuss carryover of unused tonnage capped at one quarter. I want to be clear about what this concession means: it is a structural change to the measure as notified, made on the strength of your principal supplying interest, and we make it in one move rather than three.

Second, volume. Your opening of 3 million tonnes against a pool would not survive the Council — I say that not as theatre but as fact, and I will not waste your time pretending otherwise. Equally, we accept that 400,000 tonnes is not compensatory for a principal supplier of your scale. The EU is prepared to explore a total pool in the region of 1.1 million tonnes, with a UK tranche of 900,000 tonnes within it. That is a near-tripling of the notified pool, and a UK share that recognises your concentrated trade while leaving room for other supplying interests — Turkey, Korea, India and Japan all hold reservations in this process, and the pool must be defensible to them as well as to you. We cannot approach your 2.4 million figure; there is no configuration of this measure in which full representative-period volumes continue at zero duty, and it would help us both if London's expectations were calibrated accordingly.

Third, the out-of-quota rate. 15 per cent is not a negotiating position we can engage with; it would render the bound rate ornamental. We are prepared to explore a rate of 30 per cent — a substantial move from 50 — and we note that within a country-specific tranche sized as proposed, the out-of-quota rate binds far less trade for you than under the notified design.

Fourth, duration and review. We propose five years, with a mandatory review at mid-term — year three — covering quota volumes, allocation and the out-of-quota rate. We hear your preference for three years; our counter is that a longer initial duration with a real mid-term review gives your producers more predictability, not less, and we would ask you to weigh that.

Fifth, the FTA interaction. We have heard you, and we have heard what you did not quite say about other partners. The EU is prepared to revisit the scope of the proposed clause as part of an overall settlement — including, conceivably, arrangements that preserve the operation of TCA preferences within the UK tranche. I am not tabling withdrawal today, and I will be honest that any movement on this clause will need to be matched by movement from you on volume and rate. But it is on the table as a live element of a balanced package, and I would suggest that resolving it here, quietly, is greatly preferable to the alternative for both of us.

Sixth, parallel treatment. We are ready to discuss, informally alongside this negotiation, the treatment of EU exporters under your own measure. Our expectation in a balanced outcome would be the preservation of existing EU country-specific allocations at current volumes, with no shift to global first-come, first-served on your side. We see this as mutual predictability between two partners facing the same shock, not as a concession extracted in either direction.

Finally, carve-outs. Please table your list. We commit to examining it seriously, though I can make no commitments today.

I would remind us both of the calendar: this needs to conclude by June, and the alternative to agreement is the notified measure — 400,000 tonnes, global, first-come first-served, at 50 per cent. Neither of us wants to explain that outcome to our industries. We have moved substantially today. We look for comparable movement from the United Kingdom.

private_rationale: This is the sequenced first move Brussels authorised: concede allocation fully and early (cheap for us, existential for them, and it genuinely serves the measure's anti-circumvention logic), then table numbers at the conservative end of my envelope (1.1Mt pool / 900k tranche / 30% OQR against ceilings of 1.3Mt / 1.0Mt / floor 25%), preserving 200k pool, 100k tranche and 5 percentage points of OQR as my remaining room for Rounds 3–4. I deliberately framed the tranche as constrained by Turkey/Korea/India/Japan reservations — true, and a useful brake on UK tranche inflation that doesn't come out of member-state politics. On the FTA clause I offered scope limitation ('TCA preferences operate within the tranche') rather than withdrawal: it directly defuses the joint-dispute risk by giving the UK a face-saving resolution, while holding full withdrawal as an endgame trade. I held compensation lines and carve-outs entirely in reserve per instructions — those are my closing tools if volume/rate movement alone can't land it in Round 4. The June deadline and the no-deal outcome (400k FCFS at 50%) were stated openly because time pressure is my strongest lever on a counterpart whose industry has far more to lose from no deal than mine does.

public_message:
Thank you. The United Kingdom recognises that the EU has made a genuine structural move today, and I want to acknowledge it plainly: the shift from global first-come, first-served to country-specific allocation with licensing and quarterly release is the correct architecture, and we accept that architecture as the basis for further discussion. We also note the willingness to discuss carryover, capped at one quarter — that is a sensible design point and we can work with it. And we will table our carve-out list this week; we welcome your commitment to examine it seriously.

But I must be equally plain about the distance that remains, because it is large. A UK tranche of 900,000 tonnes is 37 per cent of our representative-period trade. You describe it as recognising our concentrated position; in fact it eliminates 1.5 million tonnes a year of established market-economy trade and replaces it with a 30 per cent out-of-quota rate that no steel product in these categories can bear. I would also gently push back on the framing that the pool must be defended to Turkey and Korea: they ship larger volumes than we do across a broad product range, but the UK's volumes are concentrated on a narrow set of lines where we are frequently the dominant or only significant external supplier. Principal supplying interest is assessed on the affected trade, and on these lines that is us. The United Kingdom's position on volume therefore stands: a total pool of 3 million tonnes with a UK tranche of 2.4 million, reflecting the representative period. On the out-of-quota rate, our position also stands at 15 per cent. I hear what you say about the Council, but I would ask you to hear what I say about London: a package at or near today's numbers is not one I can carry home as compensation of substantially equivalent value, which is what Article XXVIII requires.

On duration and review: we note the five-year proposal with a mandatory mid-term review. A longer initial duration with a review that has real teeth — a defined obligation to recalibrate volumes against actual trade flows and the overcapacity picture, not a procedural box-ticking exercise — has attractions, and we are prepared to engage on that construct. On the FTA interaction: I welcome that the clause is now explicitly a live element. But I must be precise about what would resolve it. Preserving TCA preferences only within the UK tranche does not cure the breach — it codifies it. UK-originating steel above the tranche would still face disapplied preferences that the TCA guarantees. The clean solution is withdrawal of the clause, and I would again counsel that resolving it here, quietly, as you put it, means withdrawal, not redesign. Our marker stands, as do our reserved rights.

On parallel treatment: the United Kingdom is ready to begin informal discussions alongside this negotiation on the treatment of EU exporters under our own measure, and I can confirm at the level of principle that reciprocal predictability — including the preservation of country-specific allocations rather than any shift toward global first-come, first-served — is available as part of an overall balance. That availability is contingent on a UK tranche approaching representative-period volumes and on withdrawal of the FTA disapplication. I am not tabling numbers on our side today, as you are not tabling withdrawal on yours.

We have heard the EU move on structure. We now need to see the same seriousness on scale. We remain ready to work at pace — the calendar is no friendlier to us than to you.

other_terms: Import licensing with quarterly release and carryover of unused tonnage (one-quarter cap workable)
Withdrawal — not narrowing — of the clause disapplying FTA tariff reductions for UK-originating steel; UK reserves all TCA rights
Carve-out list of lines where UK supply is dominant and EU domestic production minimal to be tabled this week

In-principle, non-quantified linkage: preservation of EU country-specific allocations under the UK steel measure contingent on UK tranche near representative volumes and withdrawal of FTA disapplication
Openness to a longer duration only if the review clause carries a defined obligation to recalibrate volumes against actual trade

expectations.what_you_expect_next: Frustration that we did not move after their structural concession, followed by pressure to table a revised volume figure in Round 3. They will likely hold at ~1.1Mt/900kt through early Round 3 and test whether our 2.4Mt is a real red line or an anchor.
expectations.why: They moved on architecture precisely to trigger reciprocal movement on numbers; London has instructed me to hold, so the next tension is theirs to manage against the June deadline.

expectations.what_you_expect_next: A request for my assessment of the EU's real landing zone and a decision on when and how far to move off 2.4Mt — likely in Round 3, with volume traded against rate, TCA withdrawal and the reciprocal-treatment linkage as a package.
expectations.why: London authorised holding through Round 2 only; the EU has now put concrete numbers on the table, so the next consultation will be about the shape of the endgame, and I need London's internal landing zone before Round 3.

expectations.what_you_expect_next: Renewed pressure to join a coordinated FTA dispute now that the EU has kept the disapplication clause alive, even in narrowed form.
expectations.why: The EU's 'preserve preferences within the tranche' formula confirms the clause survives the negotiation unless traded away, which strengthens Tokyo and Seoul's argument that Article XXVIII talks alone will not remove it.

private_rationale: London's instruction is explicit: hold the full opening position through Round 2 and make the EU move first on numbers, which they have now done (1.1Mt pool, 900kt tranche, 30%, five years with mid-term review). Conceding anything this round would be pocketed and bid against, and the EU's own behaviour — a large structural concession delivered in one move, plus a candid admission that 400kt is not compensatory — confirms both that they have more room and that their June deadline is biting. My counter therefore restates the opening figures while doing three useful things at zero cost: (1) locking in their allocation/licensing/carryover concession as agreed architecture so it cannot be walked back; (2) sharpening the TCA demand from 'narrowing' to 'withdrawal', since their 'preferences within the tranche' formula is a trap that would codify the breach; and (3) making the reciprocal-treatment linkage formally contingent and non-quantified, exactly per London's authority, so they cannot price our side before pricing theirs. The five-year-with-review signal is a deliberate low-cost engagement hook — duration is our most tradable element and showing conditional flexibility there buys goodwill without moving volume or rate. The risk is that the EU reads our immobility as intransigence and hardens; I mitigate that by acknowledging their move warmly and framing our hold as grounded in trade data and the Article XXVIII 'substantially equivalent value' standard, not obstinacy. Round 3 is when movement must begin, and I will need London's landing zone before then.

report: Round 2: I tabled the authorised move — country-specific allocation with licensing and quarterly release (carryover capped at one quarter), an exploratory total pool of 1.1Mt with a 900,000t UK tranche, OQR of 30%, five-year duration with mandatory mid-term review, explicit flexibility on the FTA-disapplication clause (including possible preservation of TCA preferences within the UK tranche), informal parallel engagement on the UK safeguard measure, and a request for their carve-out list. The UK acknowledged the structural move as genuine and accepted the country-specific/licensing architecture as the basis for discussion — a real achievement: the design of the measure is now settled and it is our preferred design. But they did not move a single figure: they restated 3Mt pool / 2.4Mt UK tranche / 15% OQR in full, arguing that a 900,000t tranche (37% of their representative trade) cannot be described in London as substantially equivalent compensation, and pushed back on my 'other suppliers' framing by stressing their dominance on the specific lines at issue. On duration they engaged constructively: they are open to five years if the mid-term review has 'real teeth' — a defined obligation to recalibrate volumes against actual trade and the overcapacity picture. On the FTA clause they were precise and firm: preserving preferences within the tranche 'codifies the breach'; only full withdrawal resolves it, and their reserved rights stand. On parallel treatment they confirmed reciprocal predictability for EU exporters (preservation of country-specific allocations, no FCFS shift) is available — but explicitly contingent on a tranche approaching representative-period volumes and on withdrawal of the FTA clause. They will table the carve-out list this week. Net position: architecture agreed, but the UK is holding a hard line on scale and has constructed a two-part price (volume near 2.4Mt + clause withdrawal) for the safeguard linkage.

recommendation.reasoning: Neither side has moved on numbers, but the negotiation is on track: structure is settled, both sides are engaging, and the UK has revealed its real priorities — volume, the review's teeth, and clause withdrawal. The UK cannot actually expect 2.4Mt/15%; their refusal to move in Round 2 is standard mid-negotiation rigidity, not a walk-away signal (they explicitly reaffirmed pace and the June deadline). We hold two unused assets: the FTA-clause withdrawal and compensation lines, plus their carve-out list arrives soon. The landing zone I now see is roughly: pool 1.3–1.6Mt, UK tranche 1.1–1.4Mt, OQR 22–28%, five years with a substantive review clause, withdrawal or near-withdrawal of the FTA clause traded against volume discipline and safeguard predictability for EU exporters. I need expanded authority to move on volume in Round 3 — the UK has told us plainly that scale, not structure, is now the test, and tabling the same numbers again would stall the process with the clock running.

requests.what_you_are_asking_for: Expanded volume authority for Round 3: pool up to ~1.5Mt and UK tranche up to ~1.2Mt, ideally with headroom to 1.4Mt in reserve for Round 4
requests.why: The UK has made volume the explicit test of seriousness and has linked both the safeguard outcome and the FTA-clause question to a tranche 'approaching representative-period volumes'. My current ceiling (1.0Mt) is below anything they can carry to London; without a visible move on scale in Round 3 the negotiation stalls two rounds from the deadline. A staged increase (e.g., table 1.2Mt, hold 1.3–1.4Mt for the endgame, sweetened with carryover and carve-outs) keeps us far from their 2.4Mt while giving them something sellable as roughly half of representative trade.

requests.what_you_are_asking_for: Authority to offer full withdrawal of the FTA-disapplication clause (for the UK, or genuinely for all FTA partners) as a traded concession in Round 3 or 4, rather than scope-limitation only
requests.why: The UK stated precisely that preserving preferences within the tranche codifies rather than cures the breach, and their linkage offer is explicitly conditioned on withdrawal. Scope-limitation therefore buys nothing. Withdrawal is our largest single chip and their clearest ask; traded against a lower UK tranche, OQR discipline and EU safeguard predictability, it also removes the joint FTA-dispute risk with Japan and Korea that would damage us far beyond this file. I need the authority before I can credibly shape the endgame package.

requests.what_you_are_asking_for: Guidance on how much substance the mid-term review clause can carry: can it include a defined obligation to recalibrate volumes against actual trade flows and overcapacity data, with a presumption of adjustment?
requests.why: The UK signalled openness to five-year duration specifically if the review has teeth. A substantive review clause is cheap for us (it preserves the measure while offering the UK a credible path to volume growth) and may substitute for some immediate tonnage — a valuable currency for closing the volume gap without conceding it all up front.

requests.what_you_are_asking_for: The pre-cleared compensation line list, plus authority to use carve-outs selectively once the UK tables its list
requests.why: The UK list arrives this week. Carve-outs on lines where the UK is dominant and EU production minimal cost our industry little and count directly toward 'substantially equivalent' compensation; combined with one or two lines elsewhere in the schedule, they may be what closes the gap between a 1.2–1.4Mt tranche and their 2.4Mt demand. I will not table them in Round 3, but I need them ready for the Round 4 endgame.

requests.what_you_are_asking_for: Confirmation that I may convert the informal safeguard linkage into a mutual understanding (preservation of EU country-specific allocations at current volumes, no FCFS shift) as part of the settlement package
requests.why: The UK has made the linkage explicit and conditional on volume and clause withdrawal — the same elements we will be trading anyway. If Brussels wants this benefit locked in rather than left as atmospherics, I need to know the acceptable form (exchange of letters, joint statement, or simply reciprocal unilateral practice) before the final round.

private_rationale: My honest reading: the UK played Round 2 correctly — bank the structural concession, move nothing, and set a two-part price for their own chips. Their 2.4Mt/15% line is untenable and they know it; the real negotiation is now about where between 900,000t and 2.4Mt the tranche lands, and whether the FTA clause survives. I expect the true UK landing zone is 1.4–1.8Mt with clause withdrawal and a toothed review; ours is probably 1.2–1.4Mt with the clause diluted rather than withdrawn. The overlap exists but only just. Two risks worry me: first, if Brussels holds the 1.0Mt ceiling, the UK will escalate the TCA dispute track — and with Japan and Korea reportedly encouraging a joint FTA dispute, withdrawal of the clause may be worth more to us as dispute-avoidance than it costs us in steel terms; second, Turkey and Korea ship more than the UK and will benchmark their claims against whatever tranche we give London — every tonne we add here raises the cost of the parallel processes, which Brussels should factor into the ceiling it gives me. I have not shared either concern with the UK. The June deadline cuts against us harder than against them: no-deal costs their industry more in absolute terms, but procedurally the EU is the party that must conclude, and a failed negotiation followed by UK retaliation and a multi-partner FTA dispute would be read in Geneva as an EU process failure on my watch.

instruction: Solid work — getting the country-specific licensing architecture accepted as the basis of discussion is the single most important outcome so far, and it protects the measure's core operation. Round 3 is now about scale, and you are authorised to move, in a sequenced way. First, table a visible move on volume: total pool of 1.3 million tonnes with a UK tranche of 1.15 million tonnes. Present it as the second substantial EU move in as many rounds and demand reciprocal movement: their 2.4Mt/15% restatement cannot stand if this is to conclude. Hold reserve headroom (pool up to 1.5Mt, tranche up to 1.2Mt) for later in Round 3 only if they move materially off their opening numbers; do not table the reserve as an opening. Second, on the FTA-disapplication clause: you are now authorised to put full withdrawal on the table as a traded concession — but only as part of a package, and only against three things together: (a) UK acceptance of a tranche no higher than 1.2Mt, (b) an out-of-quota rate no lower than 25%, and (c) a locked-in mutual understanding on their safeguard measure. Signal that withdrawal is genuinely available, because scope-limitation has been rejected and holding the clause buys us a joint FTA dispute with partners beyond the UK. Do not withdraw it unilaterally or for partial movement. Third, on the review clause: you may offer real teeth — a defined obligation at mid-term to recalibrate quota volumes against actual trade flows and overcapacity data, with a presumption of adjustment. Make the adjustment symmetric in design (volumes can move up or down with the evidence) and resist any automatic entitlement to specific tonnage; the recalibration must remain subject to the measure's protective purpose. This is your cheapest currency for closing the volume gap — use it generously. Fourth, do not table compensation lines or carve-out commitments in Round 3; when their carve-out list arrives, examine it and identify which lines cost EU producers least, but hold the response for Round 4. Fifth, posture: remind them that they have now received two structural moves and zero numerical movement of their own, that a tranche above ~1.2Mt cannot pass the Council regardless of what you and I agree, and that the June deadline punishes their industry more than ours. Keep the tone constructive but make the Council constraint vivid and specific.

authority.notes: Round 3 tabling: open with pool 1.3Mt / UK tranche 1.15Mt / OQR 30% held or moved toward 28%; reserve headroom to pool 1.5Mt and tranche 1.2Mt may be used only against visible UK movement off 2.4Mt/15%. OQR floor is 25% — no exceptions this round; 22-24% may be revisited for Round 4 only as part of a full package including clause withdrawal and will need fresh clearance. FTA-disapplication clause: full withdrawal authorised as a traded concession, conditional on tranche ≤1.2Mt, OQR ≥25%, and a locked-in safeguard understanding; withdrawal should apply to the UK and may be extended to all FTA partners if that is cleaner legally and politically — flag to me before committing to the broader form. Review clause: may include a binding mid-term recalibration obligation against trade-flow and overcapacity data with a presumption of adjustment, symmetric in design, no automatic tonnage entitlements. Carryover capped at one quarter stands. Duration fixed at 5 years. Safeguard linkage: authorised to convert into a mutual understanding (exchange of letters preferred; joint statement acceptable) preserving EU country-specific allocations under the UK measure at current volumes with no shift to FCFS — no formal treaty-style linkage. Carve-outs and compensation lines: still hold for Round 4; analysis only this round.

response_to_requests.why: Authorised. An exchange of letters preserving EU country-specific allocations at current volumes with no FCFS shift is the preferred form; a joint statement is acceptable. private_rationale: My real assessment: the landing zone is pool ~1.4-1.5Mt, UK tranche ~1.2-1.3Mt, OQR 25%, five years with a toothed review, clause withdrawal, safeguard exchange of letters, plus carve-outs worth a few hundred thousand tonnes of effective access. The UK's refusal to move any number in Round 2 is rigidity, not a walk signal, but I need them off 2.4Mt/15% in Round 3 or Round 4 becomes a cliff-edge. The clause withdrawal is the key that unlocks their movement, which is why it must be presented as available but package-conditional. I will accept a deal at tranche 1.2Mt/OQR 25% with the full package; above ~1.35Mt tranche I would need TPC cover and probably additional carve-out compensation to steel member states. No-deal is tolerable for us economically but misses the June Council vote and invites the US retaliation threat to compound — I want the deal, on these terms.

report: Round 2 produced the EU's first substantive move, but no package London could accept. The EU abandoned global first-come, first-served allocation and proposed country-specific quotas administered through import licensing with quarterly release, with possible carryover capped at one quarter. It offered a total pool of 1.1 million tonnes, including a UK tranche of 900,000 tonnes; a 30% out-of-quota rate; and a five-year duration with a mandatory year-three review covering volumes, allocation and the rate. It also indicated that the FTA-disapplication clause is open to revision, but only floated preserving TCA preferences within the UK tranche. That would leave UK-originating steel above the tranche subject to disapplied TCA preferences and would not cure the breach. The EU linked movement on the clause to UK movement on volume and rate, sought preservation of existing EU country-specific allocations under the UK safeguard, and asked for our carve-out list. I acknowledged the EU's movement on architecture and undertook to table the list, but held the UK position at a 3 million tonne total pool, a 2.4 million tonne UK tranche and a 15% out-of-quota rate. I made clear that withdrawal, rather than redesign, is the clean resolution of the TCA breach, and confirmed only in principle that reciprocal predictability for EU exporters is available if the EU provides a tranche approaching representative-period volumes and withdraws the disapplication clause. No terms were agreed.

recommendation.reasoning: The current EU offer would still eliminate roughly 1.5 million tonnes of established annual UK trade and cannot be characterised as substantially equivalent compensation. We should reject it and continue. For Round 3, I recommend holding the core volume and rate positions while being authorised to accept a five-year duration, but only if the review has defined trade-flow and overcapacity triggers and forms part of a package including withdrawal of the FTA-disapplication clause. Accepting the longer duration and one-quarter carryover cap would answer the EU's call for movement without conceding the existential issue of access. We should not trade away volume merely to secure correction of a TCA breach, nor make any concession on the UK safeguard before the EU prices its own linkage.

requests.what_you_are_asking_for: Authority, at a trigger point to be set by London, to offer preservation of existing EU country-specific allocations under the UK safeguard for the same duration and review period, contingent on withdrawal of the FTA-disapplication clause and a UK tranche approaching representative-period volumes.
requests.why: This is our strongest reciprocal leverage because EU steel exports to the UK exceed UK exports to the EU. It must not be quantified or conceded before the EU improves its own offer.

requests.what_you_are_asking_for: Final approval of the carve-out list, including representative-period UK trade by line, EU domestic production data and any acceptable substitutions.
requests.why: Properly targeted carve-outs may protect the most exposed UK plants without requiring the entire representative-period volume to sit inside the quota, but I need a defensible line-by-line position before tabling it.

requests.what_you_are_asking_for: Confirmation that I should maintain controlled ambiguity with Japan and Korea: shared legal concern over FTA disapplication, but no commitment to a joint dispute or coordinated retaliation.
requests.why: The perception of possible coordinated FTA-partner escalation increases pressure on the EU at no present cost, while an explicit threat we may not execute would damage credibility and my wider committee relationships.

requests.what_you_are_asking_for: Instructions to begin contingency work on substantially equivalent UK withdrawals if no settlement is reached, without authorising me to threaten retaliation at the table yet.
requests.why: The six-month implementation delay means London needs a credible fallback ready. Keeping it out of the room for now preserves the cooperative tone while the EU's deadline continues to work in our favour.

instruction: Round 3 posture: hold on volume and rate, move visibly on duration. You may accept five years with a mandatory mid-term review, but only if the review is criteria-based — defined triggers referencing actual trade flows and overcapacity indicators, with express authority to revise volume, allocation and the out-of-quota rate, not a procedural exercise. Accept the one-quarter carryover cap as part of that construct. Present these together as our answer to their call for comparable movement, and be explicit that this is the extent of movement available until the EU moves materially on scale. Hold the 3Mt pool, 2.4Mt UK tranche and 15% rate as stated positions. Do not table any lower volume number this round. However, you may signal — clearly framed as conditional and endgame-only — that London could engage on the volume figure within a package that includes (a) withdrawal, not redesign, of the FTA disapplication clause, (b) meaningful movement on the out-of-quota rate below 30%, and (c) progress on our carve-out list. Table the carve-out list as approved (attached by e-mail; lead with the lines where UK supply is dominant and EU production minimal, with representative-period trade data per line). On the TCA: maintain the withdrawal marker; reiterate that preferences-within-tranche codifies the breach rather than curing it. On safeguard linkage: you may now confirm in principle that preservation of existing EU country-specific allocations under the UK measure, for the same duration and review period, is available — but only against withdrawal of the disapplication clause and a UK tranche approaching representative volumes. Table no tonnage figures on our safeguard. Do not threaten retaliation; do not reference our contingency work. Tone: we have moved; the ball on scale is with them; the June calendar is theirs to manage.

authority.notes: Round 3: no authority to agree any volume or rate figure — hold at 3Mt pool / 2.4Mt UK tranche / 15%. Five-year duration with mandatory criteria-based mid-term review and one-quarter carryover cap is authorised and should be offered as our movement this round. Internal landing zone, NOT for disclosure: minimum acceptable UK tranche 1.8Mt (target 2.0Mt+); maximum tolerable out-of-quota rate 20% (target 15-18%); well-targeted carve-outs can offset up to roughly 300-400kt of tranche shortfall on the most exposed lines; compensation elsewhere in the EU schedule can supplement but not substitute for tranche volume. Any package below 1.8Mt tranche or above 20% rate requires referral to London regardless of round. Withdrawal of the FTA disapplication clause is a required element of any settlement — do not accept redesign variants without referral. Safeguard linkage trigger: if the EU offers a UK tranche at or above 1.4Mt OR tables withdrawal of the disapplication clause, you may confirm in-principle preservation of existing EU country-specific allocations under the UK safeguard for matching duration/review — no UK tonnage figures without further authority.

response_to_requests.why: The EU's architecture move is real but does not compensate for a 63% cut in established trade. Hold volume and rate; our movement this round comes on duration and review instead, which answers their 'comparable movement' call without touching the existential element.

response_to_requests.request: Authority to accept five years with a mandatory, criteria-based mid-term review covering volume, allocation and rate.
response_to_requests.why: Concede duration — it is genuinely worth something to them (predictability, Council optics) and costs us little if the review has teeth. Insist on defined trade-flow and overcapacity triggers and express power to revise all three parameters; a procedural review is not acceptable.
