response_to_requests.why: Work has begun here on the candidate withdrawal list, sized to the trade impact of the notified measure. Keep it entirely out of the room for now — the cooperative tone and their June deadline are working for us. You will be told if and when a controlled signal becomes useful, likely only in Round 4.

private_rationale: The EU moved on structure faster than expected, which suggests their mandate has more room than the 900kt tranche implies — that number was framed around defensibility to Turkey and Korea, not around their true ceiling. Our job in Round 3 is to make them spend their remaining flexibility on volume and rate by giving them the one thing we can afford: duration. The 1.8Mt floor is set with the two at-risk plants in mind — below that, even with carve-outs, the Minister's subsidisation fallback becomes the live option and the negotiation is arguably not worth concluding on those terms. If Round 4 lands at 1.8-2.0Mt tranche, 15-20% rate, clause withdrawn, safeguard preservation traded, and meaningful carve-outs, that is a package I can defend to the Secretary of State and the industry as substantially equivalent in the round. The six-month retaliation delay and their Council deadline mean time is on our side; the risk is Geneva getting deal-fever in Round 4, hence the hard referral requirement below 1.8Mt.

reasoning: No settlement is currently available: the UK has accepted the country-specific licensing architecture as the basis for discussion but has expressly rejected the EU's indicative volume and out-of-quota-rate figures and continues to seek a 2.4 million tonne UK tranche at 15%. The EU should continue into Round 3 with the authorised move toward a 1.3 million tonne pool and 1.15 million tonne UK tranche, while reserving further movement for reciprocal UK concessions and a package including withdrawal of the FTA-disapplication clause, a substantive review mechanism and safeguard predictability for EU exporters.

The EU's Round 2 move on architecture (country-specific allocation, licensing, quarterly release, carryover cap, five-year duration with mandatory mid-term review) is valuable and I have acknowledged it, but the scale of the package on the table is not acceptable. A 900,000-tonne UK tranche is 37% of representative-period trade and would eliminate roughly 1.5 million tonnes a year of established market-economy exports, replaced by a 30% out-of-quota rate no product in these categories can bear. That cannot be characterised to London, ministers or the industry as substantially equivalent compensation under Article XXVIII, and it falls far below my instructed landing zone (minimum 1.8Mt tranche, maximum 20% rate). Accepting now would also forfeit the EU's remaining movement on the FTA disapplication clause and the safeguard linkage, both of which are explicitly priced but not yet tabled. London has instructed me to hold at 3Mt pool / 2.4Mt tranche / 15% through Round 3 while offering authorised movement on duration and carryover. With two rounds left, the EU's June Council deadline working against them, and my fallback being only the notified terms I already face, continuing is clearly the right call.

public_message:
Thank you. The European Union comes to Round 3 with a further substantive move, and I will be direct about what it represents: this is the second round in succession in which the EU has moved and the United Kingdom has restated its opening in full. I say that not to score a point but because London should understand the arithmetic of this room — movement on one side only does not conclude a negotiation, and we are now two rounds from the deadline.

First, volume. We have heard you that scale, not structure, is now the test. The EU is therefore prepared to move to a total pool of 1.3 million tonnes, with a UK tranche of 1.15 million tonnes within it. That is more than three times the notified pool, and a UK tranche approaching half of your representative-period trade — I put it that way deliberately, because you described the previous figure as 37 per cent, and I want the record to show the direction and pace of travel. On the out-of-quota rate, we are prepared to move to 28 per cent. I will be equally direct about the limits: a UK tranche of 2.4 million tonnes and a rate of 15 per cent cannot pass the Council in any configuration. That is not a negotiating posture; it is the constitutional reality of our side of the table, and every round spent restating it is a round lost.

Second, the review clause — and here I think we can give you something of real value. You asked for teeth rather than box-ticking, and we agree. The EU proposes a binding mid-term review with a defined obligation to recalibrate quota volumes against actual trade flows and overcapacity data, with a presumption of adjustment where the evidence supports it. The recalibration would be symmetric in design — volumes responsive to the evidence in either direction — and subject to the measure's protective purpose, so it cannot contain automatic entitlements to specific tonnage. But I want to be clear about what this offers your producers: a credible, legally grounded pathway to volume growth over the life of the measure, which a static three-year quota at any number would not.

Third, the FTA interaction. You told us last round that preserving preferences within the tranche codifies rather than cures the breach, and that only withdrawal resolves it. We have heard that precisely. The European Union is prepared to put full withdrawal of the disapplication clause on the table — genuinely, not as atmospherics. But it is the largest single element of this package, and it can only move as part of the whole: alongside a tranche within the range I have described, an out-of-quota rate no lower than 25 per cent, and the parallel understanding on your own measure that we discussed. I would also observe, as friends, that withdrawal resolves this cleanly for everyone — for the UK, and for the wider circle of partners watching this negotiation. The alternative path benefits no one at this table.

Fourth, parallel treatment. We are ready to convert our informal discussions into a mutual understanding — an exchange of letters recording the preservation of EU country-specific allocations under your measure at current volumes, with no shift to global first-come, first-served, mirroring the architecture you have accepted here. That is reciprocal predictability in its concrete form, and we are prepared to lock it in as part of the settlement.

Fifth, we look forward to receiving your carve-out list, and we confirm again that it will be examined seriously as part of the endgame package.

So the shape before us is this: country-specific allocation by licensing, as agreed; a pool of 1.3 million tonnes with a UK tranche of 1.15 million; 28 per cent out-of-quota; five years with a genuinely binding mid-term recalibration; carryover capped at one quarter; withdrawal of the FTA clause as part of the package; and a mutual understanding on your safeguard measure. We have now moved on structure, volume, rate and the clause. We need to see the United Kingdom move on scale — materially, this round — if we are to conclude by June. We stand ready to work.

expectations.what_you_expect_next: First numerical movement off the 2.4Mt/15% opening — most likely a counter in the 1.6–2.0Mt tranche range with OQR around 20%, testing whether our 1.15Mt is our ceiling. They will probe the conditions attached to clause withdrawal and may table their carve-out list now to add weight.
expectations.why: They have been told bluntly that restating their opening will not conclude this; the clause-withdrawal signal gives them a concrete reason to engage on the package rather than hold; and with one round left after this, their negotiator needs something to take to London that shows traction.

expectations.what_you_expect_next: Internal argument over whether ~1.2Mt plus clause withdrawal plus a binding review is sellable as substantially equivalent compensation; likely authorisation for their Geneva seat to move, but not to accept — London will want to test our reserve headroom in Round 4.
expectations.why: A tranche near half of representative trade is painful for their industry but the clause withdrawal and safeguard linkage give their ministers political cover; however, no capital concedes early when one round remains.

private_rationale: Executing Brussels' Round 3 instruction exactly: table the visible move (1.3Mt pool / 1.15Mt tranche / 28%) while holding the 1.5Mt/1.2Mt reserve against UK movement, signal genuine availability of full clause withdrawal but only against the three-part package, deploy the binding review clause as cheap currency, and convert the safeguard linkage into a concrete exchange-of-letters offer. The 'approaching half of representative trade' framing is deliberate — it pre-positions the narrative for a Round 4 landing at 1.2Mt, which is 50% of 2.4Mt, a number London can present as principled rather than arbitrary. I kept OQR at 28% rather than 30% to show rate movement alongside volume movement, making the package feel balanced and giving the UK something on two axes; the 25% floor is preserved and flagged as the condition for clause withdrawal. I did not table the reserve tranche (1.2Mt) because the UK has not yet moved a single figure — spending reserve now would teach them that restating their opening extracts concessions, with only one round left. The reference to 'the wider circle of partners watching' addresses the Japan/Korea joint-dispute risk without naming it at the table.

public_message: Thank you. The United Kingdom will respond in the same direct spirit. First, what we welcome, and I want to be precise because it matters: the EU has today put full withdrawal of the FTA disapplication clause on the table. That is the correct resolution of a provision that should never have been notified, and we acknowledge the political weight of it. We also welcome the review construct you describe — a binding mid-term recalibration against actual trade flows and overcapacity data, symmetric in design, with a presumption of adjustment where the evidence supports it. That is the teeth we asked for, and on that basis the United Kingdom can move today on duration and administration: we accept five years, with the mid-term review as you have described it, and we accept carryover capped at one quarter. I table our carve-out list today, with representative-period trade data per line, leading with lines where UK supply is dominant and EU domestic production is minimal. We ask that it be treated as a core element of the endgame package, not an annex to it. And on parallel treatment: the EU having now tabled withdrawal of the clause, I can confirm — in principle, and without prejudice to tonnages — that preservation of existing EU country-specific allocations under the UK measure, for a matching duration and review period, is available as part of an overall settlement. That is a significant confirmation, and it reflects the direction this negotiation should be travelling. Now the harder part. You say movement has been one-sided; I would say the movement so far has been on architecture and legal hygiene, and that on the element that determines whether the UK steel industry survives — scale — the EU has moved from 37 per cent of our established trade to 48 per cent. A tranche of 1.15 million tonnes at a 28 per cent out-of-quota rate still eliminates more than half of our representative-period trade and prices the remainder out of the market. That is not substantially equivalent compensation under Article XXVIII, and I could not describe it to London as such. Our position therefore stands at a 3 million tonne pool, a UK tranche of 2.4 million tonnes, and 15 per cent. But you asked for a signal that scale is discussable, and I will give you one, carefully and once: London could engage on the volume figure — I repeat, engage on it — within a package that includes full withdrawal of the clause, an out-of-quota rate meaningfully below 30 per cent, and genuine progress on our carve-out list. I would observe that withdrawal of a clause that breaches our treaty cannot itself be priced at a 25 per cent tariff on UK trade — that would be compensation for a wrong with a second wrong — but I take the packaging point in the spirit intended, and I am not closing anything. We have moved today on duration, administration and parallel treatment. The endgame is now about scale, and it belongs to both sides. We are ready to work through the coming days if that helps the calendar.

expectations.what_you_expect_next: A final-round move on scale: tranche toward 1.4-1.6Mt and rate toward 25%, with the clause withdrawal held formally conditional until we name a volume number. Possible attempt to close on their Round 3 terms plus marginal improvements, framing it as take-it-or-leave-it against the June deadline.
expectations.why: They have moved three rounds running and explicitly demanded material UK movement this round; they cannot escalate their deadline rhetoric further without either tabling their best figure or letting the process run out. Their conditional withdrawal offer shows the clause is priced and ready to trade, which means one more substantive move is in their locker.

expectations.what_you_expect_next: Either authority to engage on volume within a defined band for Round 4, or a decision on whether the internal landing zone (1.8Mt minimum tranche, 20% maximum rate, carve-outs offsetting 300-400kt) can be put to the EU as a closing position if the EU's Round 4 move reaches its neighbourhood.
expectations.why: The EU has now met the safeguard-linkage trigger and tabled every structural element we asked for; the only open question is scale. Round 4 is the last round, and I cannot conclude without a volume authority — London must either give me a number or accept that we go to no-deal.

expectations.what_you_expect_next: Renewed pressure to join a coordinated FTA dispute, possibly interpreting the EU's conditional withdrawal offer as proof that joint pressure works.
expectations.why: The EU's move on the clause will be read across Geneva as a concession extracted under legal threat; they will want to convert that perception into a joint action before the window closes. I will maintain the arm's-length ambiguity London authorised.

private_rationale: Holding volume and rate at the full opening while conceding visibly on duration, carryover and safeguard linkage follows London's Round 3 authority exactly and is the right sequencing on the merits. The EU has now tabled everything except scale — clause withdrawal, a genuinely binding review, country-specific licensing — which means Round 4 is purely a price negotiation on tranche and rate, the ground where our leverage (their June deadline, the asymmetry of our safeguard market, the 3.6Mt of EU steel we import) is strongest. Conceding a volume number now would be pocketed and bid against before the final round; the conditional signal that London 'could engage' on volume gives them what they asked for — evidence of UK movement — without spending a single tonne of authority. Confirming the safeguard linkage in principle is mandatory once the clause is on the table (the trigger is met), costs nothing because it is unquantified and contingent, and keeps their withdrawal offer alive rather than forcing them to retract it. I deliberately pushed back on pricing the clause at 25%+ — withdrawal cures a breach and bundling it to an unacceptable rate is a weak legal and moral position they will not want defended in Geneva — while staying constructive on packaging so the endgame remains open. The gap between their 1.15Mt/28% and my undisclosed floor of 1.8Mt/20% is wide, but carve-outs (worth 300-400kt on the most exposed lines) plus compensation elsewhere in the schedule narrow the effective gap, and the direction of their travel (400k to 900k to 1.15M across three rounds) suggests the Council has more room than they admit. The risk is a Round 4 ultimatum below 1.8Mt, which I must refer to London regardless — hence the expectations entry pressing for explicit volume authority before the final round.

report: Round 3 produced the negotiation's first genuine reciprocal movement, though the headline gap remains wide. I tabled the authorised second move: pool of 1.3Mt with UK tranche of 1.15Mt, OQR of 28%, the binding mid-term recalibration clause (symmetric, presumption of adjustment, no automatic entitlements), full withdrawal of the FTA-disapplication clause placed explicitly on the table as a packaged concession (conditioned on tranche ≤1.2Mt, OQR ≥25%, and the safeguard understanding), a proposed exchange of letters preserving EU country-specific allocations under the UK measure, and carryover capped at one quarter. The UK responded with real movement of its own for the first time: it accepted five-year duration with the review clause as described, accepted the carryover cap, tabled its carve-out list with trade data (led by lines where UK supply is dominant and EU production minimal — exactly the low-cost category we wanted), and confirmed in principle that preservation of EU country-specific allocations under its measure, for a matching duration and review period, is available as part of a settlement. Critically, the UK Geneva seat gave a carefully-worded signal that London 'could engage on the volume figure' within a package containing full clause withdrawal, an OQR 'meaningfully below 30 per cent', and genuine progress on carve-outs. Formally their numbers still stand at 3Mt/2.4Mt/15%, and they pushed back on pricing clause withdrawal against a 25% OQR ('compensation for a wrong with a second wrong'). Net position: architecture, duration, review, administration and the safeguard linkage are effectively agreed in shape; clause withdrawal is on the table and acknowledged by the UK as the correct resolution; the entire remaining negotiation is the volume/rate/carve-out triangle. The endgame is Round 4.

recommendation.reasoning: There is nothing yet to accept — the UK has not converged on any figure — but walking away is unwarranted: the UK has now moved on five elements and given an explicit conditional signal on volume, which is the clearest indication yet that a landing zone exists. The arithmetic of the endgame is visible: our tranche ceiling of 1.2Mt is 50% of their representative trade and the UK has said plainly it cannot carry that to London; their 2.4Mt is unreachable. The bridge is carve-outs: lines carved out entirely return to zero duty, which delivers UK tonnage outside the quota envelope and counts toward 'substantially equivalent' compensation without enlarging the pool beyond what the Council will pass. A tranche of ~1.3-1.4Mt (55-58% of representative trade) plus carve-outs on UK-dominant lines plus one or two compensation lines elsewhere in the schedule is describable in London as approaching representative-period duty-free access, while remaining defensible to our steel-producing member states. On the OQR, the UK has made 'meaningfully below 30%' a stated condition and has resisted pricing clause withdrawal against the rate; 28% is likely close to acceptable but I need floor authority below 25% for the final exchange. I recommend tabling in Round 4: pool 1.5Mt, tranche 1.35Mt, OQR 25% (with authority to 22-23% as the final closing concession), full clause withdrawal (extended to all FTA partners if cleared — this simultaneously defuses the Japan/Korea joint-dispute risk), acceptance of the cheapest half of their carve-out list, the exchange of letters on their safeguard measure, and the review clause as drafted. That package trades our last assets (reserve tonnage, OQR points, carve-outs, clause withdrawal) against UK acceptance in a single closing move.

requests.what_you_are_asking_for: Final-round settlement authority: pool up to 1.5Mt, UK tranche up to 1.4Mt (I propose tabling 1.35Mt and holding 1.4Mt as the last fifty thousand tonnes for the closing handshake), and OQR authority down to 22%, noting Brussels flagged that anything below 25% requires fresh clearance.
requests.why: Round 4 is the endgame and I cannot conclude with a ceiling of 1.2Mt/25% — the UK has stated on the record that 48% of representative trade is not substantially equivalent compensation, and their conditional signal on volume requires us to move first on scale. A tranche of 1.35-1.4Mt plus carve-outs gets to roughly two-thirds of their representative-period duty-free access, which combined with clause withdrawal and the review clause is the minimum package London can accept. The OQR gap between 25% and 22% is likely the final traded point.

requests.what_you_are_asking_for: Clearance to accept a defined subset of the UK carve-out list — specifically lines where UK supply is dominant and EU domestic production is minimal or nil — and the pre-cleared list of compensation lines elsewhere in the schedule that I requested after Round 1, with authority to table one or two of them.
requests.why: Their carve-out list is now on the table and they have asked for it to be treated as a core endgame element. Carved-out lines revert to zero duty, which is the cheapest way to close the volume gap — it costs EU producers nothing on lines where we barely produce, while delivering real tonnage to the UK outside the quota. Compensation lines are the residual gap-filler if volume, carve-outs and OQR together still fall short of what London can sign.

requests.what_you_are_asking_for: A decision on the scope of FTA-clause withdrawal: UK-only, or extended to all FTA partners (EEA excepted as notified). Brussels asked me to flag before committing to the broader form; I am formally recommending the broader form.
requests.why: Japan and Korea are reported to be pressing the UK toward a joint FTA dispute, and Turkey, Korea, India and Japan all hold reservations in this process. A UK-only withdrawal resolves the TCA breach but leaves the identical clause live against partners who have already signalled they view it the same way — the dispute risk merely relocates. Extending withdrawal to all FTA partners is legally cleaner (avoids a discriminatory carve-out within the clause), removes the joint-dispute scenario entirely, and costs us little since the clause's value was always as a bargaining chip. I need this decided before I table withdrawal in Round 4, because the UK will ask about scope.

requests.what_you_are_asking_for: Confirmation of the final form of the safeguard understanding: exchange of letters recording preservation of EU country-specific allocations under the UK measure at current volumes, matching duration (five years) and review period, with no shift to FCFS.
requests.why: The UK has now confirmed this in principle 'without prejudice to tonnages', matching duration and review. It will be part of the Round 4 package and I need to arrive with agreed text or a near-agreed text, since there will be no time to draft after the final exchange if we are to conclude by June.

private_rationale: The UK Geneva seat played Round 3 skilfully — accepting everything cheap (duration, administration, review) to bank our moves while holding 2.4Mt/15% formally, then floating the conditional volume signal to make us move first again. I do not think London's real floor is anywhere near 2.4Mt; the careful wording ('engage on the volume figure') and the fact that they confirmed the safeguard linkage in principle suggest they are pricing a package, not a number. My honest read of their minimum: a tranche above 1.3Mt, OQR at or below 25%, meaningful carve-outs, and clause withdrawal. That is inside what we can give. The two risks I am managing: (1) if I table the full reserve too early in Round 4, the UK pockets it and re-anchors, so sequencing matters — carve-outs and the OQR floor should come after they state a figure; (2) the Japan/Korea joint-dispute whisper is the thing that could blow this up from outside the room, which is why I am pushing for the broader clause withdrawal even though Brussels may see it as over-generous. On the safeguard linkage, getting EU allocations locked in an exchange of letters is a genuine win for our member states and worth real tonnage. If Round 4 fails, the fallback (400,000t global FCFS at 50%) hurts the UK far more than us, but it also guarantees UK retaliation against our exports into their market, a TCA dispute, and possibly the joint FTA dispute — so no-deal is not actually comfortable for us despite the asymmetry, and Brussels should not treat the notified measure as a good outcome. I will need to manage my own capital colleague as much as the UK in the final round.

instruction: Round 4 is the endgame and this is your settlement authority. report: Round 3 produced the EU's most significant movement yet, but the gap on scale remains the negotiation. The EU moved to a total pool of 1.3Mt with a UK tranche of 1.15Mt (up from 900kt) and a 28% out-of-quota rate (from 30%). Critically, it put full withdrawal of the FTA disapplication clause genuinely on the table — but packaged it: withdrawal only alongside a tranche in the range offered, a rate no lower than 25%, and the parallel safeguard understanding. It also proposed a binding mid-term review with a defined obligation to recalibrate volumes against actual trade flows and overcapacity data, symmetric in design with a presumption of adjustment — meeting our 'teeth not box-ticking' test, though with the caveat that it cannot contain automatic entitlements to specific tonnage and is subject to the measure's protective purpose. On parallel treatment, the EU is ready to convert informal discussions into a mutual understanding: an exchange of letters preserving EU country-specific allocations under our safeguard at current volumes, no shift to global FCFS. The EU pushed back on the symmetry of movement, noting it has moved two rounds running while we restated our opening. I responded by banking real movement: accepted five years with the binding recalibration review, accepted the one-quarter carryover cap, tabled the carve-out list, and — the safeguard trigger having been met by their tabling withdrawal — confirmed in principle that preservation of existing EU allocations under our measure for a matching duration/review is available as part of a settlement. I held 3Mt/2.4Mt/15% as stated positions but gave the authorised endgame signal, once and carefully: London could engage on the volume figure within a package including full withdrawal of the clause, a rate meaningfully below 30%, and genuine progress on carve-outs. I also put down a marker that withdrawal of a treaty-breaching clause cannot itself be priced at a 25% tariff on UK trade — compensation for a wrong with a second wrong. Where things stand: architecture (country-specific, licensing, quarterly release, carryover cap) is effectively settled; duration and review are settled at five years with binding mid-term recalibration subject to drafting; withdrawal of the clause is on the table but packaged; safeguard linkage is confirmed in principle on both sides. The open elements for Round 4 are tranche volume (1.15Mt vs our 2.4Mt stated; our floor 1.8Mt), rate (28% vs our 15% stated; our ceiling 20%), carve-outs (tabled, no EU response yet), and any compensation elsewhere in the schedule. One round remains before the June deadline.

But walking away would be worse: no-deal means the notified terms (400kt global FCFS at 50%), which London has assessed as fatal to the industry, and the EU has now demonstrated genuine momentum — three moves in two rounds, including the clause withdrawal we demanded. The correct play is a final round in which we make our first real movement on scale, from a position of having banked everything else. The negotiation has narrowed to two numbers and a list; that is a settleable endgame if both sides move in Round 4.

instruction: Round 4 is the endgame, and you have authority to close it. Posture: open by confirming what is settled — country-specific licensing architecture, quarterly release, one-quarter carryover, five years with the binding criteria-based mid-term recalibration as they described it — and state that the only open questions are two numbers and a list. Then make our move, once and clearly: the United Kingdom can state a position of a 2.0 million tonne UK tranche and an 18% out-of-quota rate, framed as a major one-time movement contingent on comparable EU movement, within a package that includes full withdrawal of the FTA disapplication clause and genuine progress on our carve-out list. On the clause: press the principled position that withdrawal corrects a legal defect and should not be priced against tariff levels — but do not die on that hill; if they insist on packaging, treat the package holistically and judge it by the numbers. Use the EU's June Council deadline: they need to conclude; the notified terms are our worst case and their political problem. Do not threaten retaliation, do not reference contingency work, do not disclose our floor or ceiling. Negotiate hard on carve-outs — press for specific line commitments, not a promise to examine. Whatever the final configuration on the table at round's end, report it verbatim; London's decision rule is set out below.

authority.notes: Landing zone (NOT for disclosure): floor 1.8Mt UK tranche, ceiling 20% out-of-quota rate. Stated position for the round: 2.0Mt tranche / 18%. Thank you. This is the final round, and I will not pretend otherwise. What I am about to table is the European Union's closing package. It is a single, indivisible whole — every element is conditional on acceptance of every other element — and it represents the outer limit of what the Council will pass. There is no Round 5, on either side of this table.

First, volume. The EU moves to a total pool of 1.5 million tonnes, with a UK tranche of 1.35 million tonnes within it. That is 56 per cent of your representative-period trade inside the quota — before carve-outs. Combined with the carve-outs I am about to describe, the package delivers roughly two-thirds of your representative-period duty-free access. I will be candid: I cannot reach 2.4 million tonnes, and no figure approaching it exists on my side of the table. What I can do is deliver the great majority of your established trade at zero duty, through the combination of tranche and carve-outs, in a form the Council can actually approve.

Second, the out-of-quota rate: 25 per cent. You asked for a rate meaningfully below 30 per cent; this is that, and it applies to a far smaller volume of your trade than under any earlier configuration.

Third, the FTA interaction. The European Union withdraws the disapplication clause in full — and I can go further than you asked: the withdrawal will extend to all FTA partners, with the EEA exception as notified. We present this not as a concession extracted by any one member, but as the EU choosing legal cleanliness and de-escalation with the wider circle of partners watching this process. The clause is gone. That question is closed, here, quietly, as we both preferred.

Fourth, carve-outs. We have examined your list seriously, as promised. The EU accepts the carve-out of the lines on which UK supply is dominant and EU domestic production is minimal or nil — taken in descending order of that ratio, up to an aggregate of 250,000 tonnes of representative-period trade. Any qualifying lines beyond that cap will receive a guaranteed share of the residual pool rather than full carve-out. These lines revert to zero duty, outside the quota entirely, permanently for the duration of the measure.

Fifth, the settled elements, which I confirm without reopening: country-specific allocation administered by licensing with quarterly release; carryover of unused tonnage capped at one quarter; five-year duration; and the binding mid-term recalibration against actual trade flows and overcapacity data, symmetric in design, with a presumption of adjustment — the teeth you asked for, as drafted.

Sixth, parallel treatment. I table near-agreed text for an exchange of letters recording the preservation of EU country-specific allocations under your steel measure at current volumes, for a matching five-year duration and review period, with no shift to global first-come, first-served. You confirmed this in principle last round; the text before you gives it concrete form.

Seventh, we hold in reserve a small number of compensation lines elsewhere in our schedule, which we are prepared to add to this package if a residual gap remains in your assessment of substantially equivalent value.

Let me be equally plain about the alternative, because the deadline makes it real. If this package is not accepted today, the notified measure proceeds: 400,000 tonnes, global first-come first-served, 50 per cent, no review clause — and your industry, which ships three-quarters of its exports into this market, carries the larger share of that outcome. Against that alternative stands a package delivering roughly two-thirds of your representative trade at zero duty, a 25 per cent ceiling on the remainder, a binding path to volume growth at mid-term, the complete removal of the FTA clause for you and every other partner, and locked-in predictability for EU exporters under your own measure. That is a settlement both capitals can defend. We ask the United Kingdom to accept it.

public_message: Thank you. The United Kingdom will respond with the same candour you have shown, and I will begin by acknowledging what is real in this package. The full withdrawal of the disapplication clause — extended to all FTA partners — is the correct outcome and we welcome it without qualification. The architecture we agreed in principle is now confirmed in detail. The carve-out commitment, reverting qualifying lines to zero duty outside the quota entirely, is genuine and we recognise it. And the review clause as described is the substantive recalibration we asked for. This is a far better measure than the one notified, and the record should show that. But I must be equally direct about the arithmetic, because Article XXVIII sets a legal test — compensation of substantially equivalent value — and on the numbers tabled, that test is not met. A tranche of 1.35 million tonnes is 56 per cent of our representative trade. With carve-outs at the 250,000-tonne cap, roughly two-thirds of our established duty-free access is preserved; the remaining third — approaching a million tonnes a year of concentrated UK trade on lines where we are frequently your dominant external supplier — faces a 25 per cent rate. That is not a margin; on most of these product categories it is a wall. The United Kingdom's position, stated once more for the record, is a UK tranche of 1.8 million tonnes and an out-of-quota rate of 20 per cent, with the carve-out commitment at or above the cap you have described. I note this would still leave the United Kingdom absorbing a very substantial loss of established trade — it is already a compromise position, and London would be defending it as such. I also take up your seventh point in the spirit in which you offered it: you held compensation lines in reserve against a residual gap in our assessment of substantially equivalent value. I confirm formally that a residual gap exists, and I ask that those lines be tabled and added to the package now, in this round, alongside the fullest possible deployment of qualifying carve-out lines within your cap. I will not accept this package at the table — I do not have the authority, and as it stands I could not recommend it. I do not reject it either. The United Kingdom reserves all its rights under Article XXVIII, as is standard. I will report the final terms — the package as tabled, and any completion of it by the compensation lines — to London faithfully and today, and the United Kingdom's decision will follow through capitals. Whatever that decision, I want to say to this delegation directly: this negotiation has been conducted properly, on both sides, and that matters beyond this file.
